title: Expense sharing like Splitwise
idea: A Splitwise design records who paid and how each expense splits, keeps one net balance per person, and settles those balances with few transfers.

analogy.text: Flatmates keep a shared notebook. Each receipt adds to the payer and subtracts each person's share. At month end, only the totals matter.
analogy.breaks: The notebook has no rules; code must reject shares that do not add up.

points: Money is a `long` in cents; `double` drifts when you split and add.
A `SplitStrategy` turns a total into shares: equal, exact, percent, and more.
The `Ledger` adds the total to the payer and subtracts each share.
`Settler` repeatedly pairs the biggest debtor with the biggest creditor.

hero.title: One expense, from receipt to settlement

steps.caption: `ana` pays 10000 cents for three people. The expense names a payer, a total and a split.
`Equal` divides by three. The one leftover cent goes to the first person, so shares sum exactly.
The ledger adds 10000 to `ana` and subtracts each share. All balances still sum to zero.
A different expense: an `Exact` split whose shares miss the total throws in the strategy. The ledger never changes.
To settle, the biggest debtor pays the biggest creditor as much as one side needs.
Each pairing zeroes at least one person, so n people need at most n − 1 transfers.

code.title: Split and record
code.caption: Two good expenses and one bad one. Balances print in name order from a `TreeMap`.

walk.text: The strategy contract: given a total, say who owes how much.
`Equal` hands the leftover cents out one each, so nothing is lost.
`Exact` refuses shares that do not add up to the total.
Ask for shares first; only a valid split touches the balances.
Positive means the group owes you; negative means you owe the group.
The third expense is rejected and leaves every balance as it was.

code.title: Settle up
code.caption: Four net balances turned into transfers by greedy pairing.

walk.text: A `Transfer` is a value: from, to and an amount in cents.
Find the biggest creditor and debtor; stop when either is missing.
Move the smaller of the two amounts, which zeroes at least one person.
`sign` lets one method find the largest credit or the largest debt.
`main` settles a set of balances that sum to zero.

pitfalls: Never store money as `double`; use `long` cents or `BigDecimal`.
Validate the split before touching balances, or a rejected expense leaves half an update.
Do not promise the fewest transfers: greedy pairing is simple, not always optimal.

quiz.why: The bad split throws before the ledger changes. `ana`'s 10000 splits 3334, 3333, 3333; then `cy`'s exact split charges 1500 and 3000.

takeaway: Split with a strategy, keep net balances in cents, settle greedily.

starters: How would I add a percentage split without touching `Ledger`?
How do groups fit in when one person is in several groups?
Why is finding the minimum number of transfers hard?
